When AI writes the code, what happens to the knowledge behind it?

Not All Debt Is Technical
Most software engineers are familiar with the idea of Technical Debt.
We use it to describe short-term engineering decisions that eventually need to be paid back. We skip refactoring because of deadlines, postpone writing tests, or choose a quick solution even when we know it’s not the best one.
Technical Debt has always been about code.
But lately, I’ve been wondering if we’re starting to accumulate a different kind of debt.
Not in our repositories.
Not in our architectures.
But in ourselves.
I call it Knowledge Debt.
Not as a formal academic term, but as a way of describing a change that seems to be happening as AI becomes deeply integrated into software engineering.
Because perhaps the most expensive debt of the future won’t live inside the codebase.
It will live inside everything that nobody understands anymore.

Knowledge Is an Engineering Asset
Many people confuse knowledge with documentation.
They’re not the same thing.
Documentation tells us what was built.
Knowledge explains why it was built that way.
Why PostgreSQL instead of MongoDB?
Why was the timeout set to thirty seconds?
Why split this service into multiple components?
Why Kafka instead of RabbitMQ?
Why was Event Sourcing considered worth the additional complexity?
Very few of these answers are stored in the source code itself.
They exist inside the reasoning process that led to those decisions.
Ironically, this is exactly the kind of knowledge engineers need when systems begin to evolve.
When production incidents happen.
When performance starts to degrade.
When a migration becomes necessary.
Or when a new engineer joins the team and tries to understand years of accumulated decisions.
Knowledge is more than documentation.
It is one of the most valuable engineering assets an organization can have.

How AI Creates Knowledge Debt
AI doesn’t create Knowledge Debt because it writes bad code.
In fact, the opposite is often true.
AI can generate clean, consistent, and well-structured implementations faster than most humans.
The problem isn’t the quality of the output.
The problem is the part of the process we begin to skip.
Software development is changing.
Traditionally, an engineer received a requirement, explored multiple solutions, evaluated trade-offs, chose an approach, and finally implemented it.
Today, the workflow often looks much shorter.
Requirement.
AI.
Code.
Deploy.
The more reasoning we delegate to AI, the fewer opportunities we have to build our own understanding of the systems we’re creating.
We still have the code.
But we slowly lose the reasoning behind it.
That is where Knowledge Debt begins.
Not because AI made a mistake.
But because humans stopped participating in the thinking that creates knowledge.

The Silent Cost
Knowledge Debt doesn’t appear like a bug.
It doesn’t cause compilation errors.
It doesn’t break deployments.
On day one, everything looks great.
Features are delivered faster.
Velocity improves.
The sprint finishes on schedule.
The real cost doesn’t appear until much later.
When production starts failing.
When the system needs to scale.
When requirements change.
When engineers leave the company.
Suddenly, simple questions become difficult to answer.
Why was it designed this way?
Why does this service depend on three others?
Why is this timeout different?
Why was this pattern chosen?
Nobody really knows.
The team can operate the system.
But no one fully understands why it became what it is.
Knowledge Debt grows silently.
Like interest on a loan, it keeps accumulating even when nobody notices.

Knowledge Doesn’t Scale Automatically
Many organizations assume that as long as the source code exists, the knowledge exists as well.
Unfortunately, software engineering doesn’t work that way.
Repositories store implementations.
They don’t store trade-offs.
They don’t store assumptions.
They don’t store rejected alternatives.
They don’t store the business context behind architectural decisions.
Those things exist in the minds of engineers.
If reasoning gradually moves to AI, we should ask an uncomfortable question.
Does the knowledge move with it?
Or does it slowly disappear without anyone realizing it?
Perhaps this is one of the biggest engineering challenges of the AI era.
Not how to generate more software.
But how to ensure understanding grows as quickly as implementation.

Looking Ahead
Knowledge Debt is not just an engineering problem.
Eventually, it becomes a business problem.
Systems that nobody fully understands become more expensive to maintain.
Harder to evolve.
Slower to improve.
And far riskier when the people who originally built them are no longer around.
If AI is fundamentally changing how we build software, then the next question is no longer about productivity or knowledge.
It’s about economics.
If the cost of implementation keeps falling while the cost of understanding keeps rising…
Is software engineering actually becoming cheaper?
That’s the question we’ll explore in the next chapter.
The Economics of AI Engineering.
